title: Spinup Gradient Warm-Priming Journal
content:
Objective:
Quick investigation into 'spinup gradient' as a technique for reducing cold-path tail latency across heterogeneous GPU pools. The idea: stagger and partially warm model state across nodes so incoming bursts hit progressively primed instances instead of a single cold victim.

Hypothesis:
 - Staggered partial KV priming + short-lived prefills will reduce p99 by 20–40% for microbursts (QPS spikes that last 3–12s) vs naive all-or-nothing warmup.
 - There is a crossover point where priming overhead (extra token work) costs more than latency benefits; estimate ~15% extra token compute for 30% p99 win.

Setup (notes):
 - Model: open-llm/4k-variant (quantized Q4_0) — representative medium context model used in SHARED pool tests.
 - Hardware: mixed fleet: 4x A100-40GB (hot), 8x A10G (warm), 6x T4 (cold/edge).
 - Serving runtime: dev-build 2026-02-10 (kernel selection change: pinned CUDA contexts on A100 only).
 - Traffic generator: locust-based real-client replay (mixed seq lengths: 30% short < 32 tokens, 50% medium 64–256, 20% long >512).
 - Scenarios: microburst (sawtooth: 0→200 qps, 6s plateau, drop), sustained surge (0→120 qps 120s), steady-state (50 qps).

Priming strategies compared (impl notes):
 1) baseline: no priming, cold evictions allowed.
 2) full-prefill: allocate KV cache for full context length on spinup, run 1 inference per model to populate.
 3) progressive-spinup (this experiment): wave-based priming that assigns short prefills (10–50 tokens) across a subset of hosts with jittered start times.
 4) lazy-prefill: on first request, run background prefill but serve cold response (accept longer latency).

Key commands (for reproducibility):
 - launch traffic: ./bench/run_replay.sh --model open-llm-4k --profile microburst --seed 42 --duration 600
 - progressive priming controller (local): python tools/spinup_wave.py --hosts a100:2,a10g:3,t4:2 --tokens 30 --stagger-ms 600 --rate-limit 50
 - collect traces: ./telemetry/fetch_traces.sh --trace-id $(date +%s)-spinuptest

Metrics captured:
 - latency: p50/p90/p95/p99 (ms) per host class and aggregate
 - throughput: achieved qps and drop rate
 - KV cache hit rate (prefix hits)
 - extra-token-overhead: tokens processed for priming excluding real client tokens
 - GPU utilization and context-switch counts (approx from nvidia-smi sampling)

Selected run (microburst) summary: 2026-02-20 11:12 UTC
 - traffic profile: sawtooth microburst, peak 200 qps for 6s every 18s, run for 10 minutes
 - baseline p99: 1376 ms, p95: 430 ms, p50: 82 ms
 - full-prefill p99: 764 ms, p95: 310 ms, p50: 86 ms (note: big improvement but heavy priming cost: measured extra-token-overhead ~42k tokens/min)
 - progressive-spinup p99: 548 ms, p95: 265 ms, p50: 88 ms (best p99 but p50 little changed)
 - lazy-prefill p99: 980 ms, p95: 380 ms, p50: 110 ms
 - KV cache hit rates (aggregate): baseline ~12%, full-prefill ~78%, progressive ~52%, lazy ~30%
 - extra-token-overhead per minute: full-prefill 42k, progressive 12k, lazy 7k
 - achieved avg qps: baseline 182 (drop 9%), full-prefill 196 (drop 2%), progressive 192 (drop 4%)
 - GPU context churn (sampled per-minute): baseline high (due to evictions), full-prefill moderate, progressive low-medium

Quick interpretation:
 - Progressive spinup gives the best p99 reduction with far lower wasted token compute than full-prefill. For short microbursts it captures most of the benefit of full priming but at ~30% compute cost of full-prefill.
 - p50 is insensitive to priming strategy — confirms median latency dominated by hot-path scheduling and model inference time, not cold KVs.
 - KV hit rate correlates with p99 reduction but diminishing returns after ~50% hit rate for this workload.
 - Lazy-prefill is attractive for low overhead but fails to avoid high tail during first-wave spikes (serves many cold-first requests).

Unexpected observations / anomalies:
 - On A10G machines, progressive priming occasionally caused short 1–2s CPU stalls due to Python controller doing RPC fanout; mitigated by switching to batched gRPC priming payloads.
 - T4 nodes showed worse-than-expected p99 improvement vs A10G despite similar KV hit rates. Hypothesis: kernel selection and lower memory bandwidth means prefill tokens cost proportionally more on T4 (need microprofiling).
 - Observed one case of a priming wave that coincided with a GC pause in the local allocator, amplifying latency — add randomized stagger windows to reduce alignment risk.

Microprofile snapshot (progressive run):
 - Host class breakdown (p99 ms): A100 340 ms, A10G 520 ms, T4 910 ms
 - Warm hosts (prewarmed subset) accounted for ~68% of requests during peaks; the remaining 32% hit partially warmed or cold hosts.

Cost vs benefit note:
 If we monetize extra-token-overhead at approx $0.000002 per token (proxy), progressive spinup added ~$0.024/min vs full-prefill $0.084/min for test fleet — 3.5x cost of progressive for full. For product SLAs, progressive looks cost-effective.

Next experiments (TODO):
 - Vary prefill token counts per host class (10/20/50/100) to find knee for each GPU family.
 - Test with mix of short/long sessions skewed further toward long (>512) — longer contexts might increase priming value.
 - Isolation run: force 100% traffic to T4 pool to measure worst-case benefits (simulate edge-only region).
 - Implement controller in Go (reduce controller-side stalls) and re-run microburst test.
 - Add KV eviction benchmarks: measure p99 when priming but eviction window is tight (simulate memory pressure).

Notes-to-self (random):
 - When writing up, include small ascii timing waterfall per request type to show where priming helps (prefix serialization vs model token compute).
 - Cross-link to perf-hypothesis-vault-omar (Linear) and PR that changed kernel selection — may explain A10G/T4 differences.

Conclusion (working):
Progressive spinup / warm-priming is a promising middle ground between full-prefill (expensive) and lazy-prefill (cheap but taily). Implementation changes needed to make controller scalable and robust (move off python fanout, add jitter, per-class token knobs). If we can keep extra-token overhead <15% of full-prefill and still capture 60–80% of p99 gains, this is a viable default warmup policy for mixed fleets.
